scenes.caption: Overview: one request through the gateway
scenes.narration: This is LLM Control Room. On the overview, Try it sends a real request through the gateway. A simple greeting goes to the cheapest model, with its cost, latency and cache result shown.
scenes.manual_full: Open the app and sign in with the admin token it prints. The Overview page has a Try it panel with four example requests. Press Greeting: the gateway routes it, and the result shows the model it picked, the cost, the gateway latency, the cache result and the reason for the route. In this run the greeting was served by nano-mock.

scenes.caption: Try it: an API key and an email are redacted before the call
scenes.narration: This request carries an API key and an email address. Both are redacted before the call leaves, and the result lists each redaction.
scenes.manual_full: Press Key + email. The prompt contains an sk- key and an email address. The gateway replaces both before the request reaches any model, and Redactions applied names each one. In this run: redacted:email, redacted:openai_key.

scenes.caption: Try it: a prompt injection is blocked, no model is called
scenes.narration: A prompt injection is refused at the door. No model is called, it costs nothing, and the findings say which rules fired.
scenes.manual_full: Press Injection. The input guardrails refuse the request with HTTP 400 before routing, so no model is called and the cost is zero. The findings list the rules that matched. In this run: injection:instruction_override, injection:obfuscated, injection:system_prompt_exfil.

scenes.caption: Tenants: a new tenant with its own key and a ready curl command
scenes.narration: Each app gets its own tenant. Creating one shows its key once, with a curl command that calls the gateway.
scenes.manual_full: Go to Tenants, type a name under New tenant and press Create with first key. The key is shown only once, next to a curl command for the OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Only a hash of the key is stored. The tenant starts with a budget and a rate limit you can change on its card.

scenes.caption: The curl command was run from a terminal; the tenant's spend updates
scenes.narration: That exact command was run from a terminal. The gateway answered, and the tenant's card now shows the spend against its budget.
scenes.manual_full: Copy the command and run it in a terminal (in Windows PowerShell type curl.exe). The reply is a normal chat completion; its x-lcr headers carry the model, cost and cache result. Reload Tenants: the card shows the call counted against the budget. In this run the command returned HTTP/1.1 200 OK; x-lcr-cache: miss, x-lcr-cost-usd: 0.00000250, x-lcr-model: nano-mock, x-lcr-trace: 7ee0cf9a66bd4e0e.

scenes.caption: Playground: a file of prompts, one row per result
scenes.narration: In the playground, a file of prompts runs as a batch. Each row shows the route, cost, cache, redactions, and any block.
scenes.manual_full: Go to Playground and drop a .jsonl, .csv or .txt file of prompts on Batch (or choose it). Pick a tenant and press Run. Each prompt gets a row with its status, model, difficulty, cost, cache result, latency, redactions and answer or refusal; the results download as CSV. In this run: 5 of 5 done, 4 served, 1 blocked, cost $0.000654, 1 cached.

scenes.caption: Router: what the same traffic would cost on the biggest model
scenes.narration: After a run of simulated traffic, the router page compares the spend with sending the same calls to the biggest model, and shows where each request went.
scenes.manual_full: The Simulator sends realistic traffic through the gateway with the built-in mock models. The Router page then shows the spend, what the same calls would cost on the baseline model, the saving, where requests went, and a matrix of estimated against intended difficulty. Cache hits are not credited to the router. In this run the router spent 83.6% less than always titan-mock.

scenes.caption: Observability: cost, latency percentiles and prompt drift
scenes.narration: Observability shows cost per tenant and model, latency percentiles, and prompt drift, without storing any prompt.
scenes.manual_full: Observability shows calls, spend, cost per successful answer, p50, p95 and p99 latency (cache hits excluded), success, grounding, cache, fallback and redaction rates, then cost per tenant, feature and model and a prompt drift score. Filter by window, tenant or feature; export the calls as CSV. In this run: p50 672 ms, p95 1.50 s.

scenes.caption: Releases: a bad canary is rolled back automatically
scenes.narration: A new prompt version went out as a canary. Its quality fell below the limit, so it was rolled back automatically.
scenes.manual_full: A release is called like a model name. Add a version and send it Canary, A/B or Shadow traffic. Each version is held to its SLO: when a challenger breaks one on its own with enough samples, auto-rollback archives it and the champion takes all traffic back. The Auto-rollback check says why. In this run: rolled back after 40 challenger calls checked.

scenes.caption: Agent runs: the run stops at its cost limit
scenes.narration: Agents run under hard limits. This one keeps paying for searches, and it is stopped before it crosses its cost limit.
scenes.manual_full: Go to Agent runs, pick a scenario, set the hard limits (steps, tool calls, cost, seconds, repeat limit) and press Run agent. Every reasoning step is a billed gateway call. The run stops at the first limit it would cross and the log says which one. In this run (cost limit $0.2): LIMIT HIT: cost (max 0.2, used 0.160), stopped before premium_search (up to $0.0400).

scenes.caption: Sandbox: twelve attacks against each hardening profile
scenes.narration: Finally, the sandbox runs twelve real attack programs. Most get through the plain subprocess, and none get through the restricted profile.
scenes.manual_full: Go to Sandbox and press Run the attack suite. Twelve attack programs run under each available profile. The harness plants a secret, listens on a loopback port and watches the disk, so got through is evidence it saw itself. The last row counts what got through each profile. In this run: 10 of 12 got through subprocess, 0 of 12 through restricted.
